crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines
children.blurb: Reproducible notebooks and pipelines cover the practices and tools that let a quantitative analysis be rerun, checked, and extended by someone else.

children.name: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
children.blurb: Asking data questions in plain language means a person types a question such as "which regions grew fastest last quarter" and a system translates it into a query against a database, spreadsheet, or data warehouse.

children.name: Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data
children.blurb: Large-scale compute on institutional data covers the use of shared high-performance and cloud computing resources to analyze datasets that an organization controls, such as clinical records, financial transactions, sensor logs, or administrative archives.

children.name: Writing Statistical Code with AI
children.blurb: Writing statistical code with AI covers the use of AI assistants, such as large language models, to help write, edit, and debug code for statistical analysis.

children.name: Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection
children.blurb: Testing a study design before data collection means checking whether a planned quantitative study can answer its research question before resources are spent gathering real data.

sections.body: Quantitative analysis and reproducible work is the part of AI research that turns data into defensible numbers. AI now helps write and refactor statistical code, generate notebook cells, suggest tests, and translate plain language questions into database queries. It can also help schedule large scale compute jobs, track dependencies, and check that a pipeline runs the same way on a new machine. In practice, these tools sit beside the researcher rather than replacing the researcher. They speed up boilerplate, catch some errors, and make it easier to share a working analysis. The field is less about a single model and more about a chain of steps that must stay honest from raw data to final table.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are solved well enough for daily use. Container images, version control, unit tests, and automated notebook execution are common and reliable when set up carefully. AI can draft a regression, a data cleaning script, or a simulation, but it often produces code that looks correct and is not. Plain language data questions still fail when the underlying schema is ambiguous or the question hides a definition. Large scale compute on institutional data runs into access controls, cost, and privacy rules that no model can wish away. Reproducibility across different machines, data versions, and institutions remains hard, and statistical validity still depends on human judgment about design, assumptions, and missing data.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages in this section form a sequence from setup to design. Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines is the foundation, covering how to make an analysis run again and again with the same inputs. Asking Data Questions in Plain Language is the front door, showing how natural language can become a query without losing the meaning of the request. Large-Scale Compute on Institutional Data deals with the execution layer, where jobs run on protected systems and where governance matters as much as speed. Writing Statistical Code with AI focuses on the modeling step, including how to test code and check that a method matches the question. Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection comes before all of that in time, using simulation and pilot checks to see whether a planned study can answer its question, and the site's library holds 135 research papers that point a reader toward the parts of that literature that match each stage.
